Foundations: customers, channels and a plan

Before you post or pay for anything, you need three things: a clear picture of who buys from you, a small set of online places where they can find you, and a goal with numbers attached. This module builds all three, using the marketing funnel as the map for the whole course.

**Marketing** is everything you do to help the right people discover your product, trust it, buy it and come back. **Traditional marketing** uses offline channels: flyers, banners, radio jingles, newspaper adverts, posters at the bus stop and word of mouth in the market. **Digital marketing** uses the internet and mobile phones: search engines such as Google, social media such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, email, WhatsApp, and online maps.
A woman standing beside a large megaphone and marketing charts
Marketing, online or offline, is about helping the right customer find you and choose you.

Digital does not replace traditional. A woman selling fabrics at Balogun Market still gains customers who walk past her stall. But digital adds three powers that a flyer does not have. First, **targeting**: you can show an advert only to people in Ibadan who are interested in weddings, instead of everyone who passes a pole. Second, **measurement**: you can see how many people saw your post, how many clicked and how many sent a message. Third, **low starting cost**: a WhatsApp Business account and a Google Business Profile are free to create, so a small business can start with only data and time.
Owned, earned and paid media

A healthy plan uses all three. Owned channels are your shop window that nobody can take away. Earned media is the most trusted, because it comes from other customers. Paid media is the fastest way to reach new people, but it stops the moment you stop paying. Many small businesses make the mistake of paying for ads before their owned channels are ready, so new visitors arrive at an empty page and leave.
The marketing funnel

The **marketing funnel** describes the journey from a stranger to a loyal customer. It is wide at the top, because many people hear about you, and narrow at the bottom, because only some of them buy. This course uses a simple four-stage version.
The four-stage marketing funnel
Awareness: they discover you
Consideration: they compare and ask
Conversion: they buy
Loyalty: they return and refer
Each stage needs different content and a different measure of success.
**Awareness**: a person sees your post, your advert or your shop on Google Maps for the first time. You measure reach: how many people saw you.
**Consideration**: she looks at your catalog, reads reviews, asks the price on WhatsApp. You measure clicks, profile visits and messages.
**Conversion**: she pays, by transfer, POS or a payment link from Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint. You measure orders and sales.
**Loyalty**: she buys again and tells her friends. You measure repeat orders and referrals.

When sales are low, the funnel helps you find where the problem is. If many people see your posts but nobody messages, the problem is in consideration: perhaps your price is hidden or your photos are poor. If many people message but few pay, the problem is in conversion: perhaps you reply too slowly or delivery is unclear.
Worked example: comparing the cost of reaching people
For example, Amaka sells small chops for parties in Port Harcourt. She has two options for a weekend promotion. All prices are illustrative and approximate.
Option A: print 500 flyers for about ₦15,000 and pay a helper about ₦5,000 to share them. Total about ₦20,000. If every flyer reaches one person, she reaches 500 people.
Cost per 1,000 people for flyers: ₦20,000 ÷ 500 × 1,000 = ₦40,000.
Option B: run a Facebook and Instagram ad for about ₦10,000. Her Ads Manager report later shows a reach of 8,000 people in Port Harcourt.
She also checks results: the flyers brought 3 orders that she can trace (she asked each caller where they heard of her), and the ad brought 5 orders through WhatsApp.

The ad reached far more people for each naira, and she could measure it directly. The flyers still worked locally, so she keeps a few for her own street and moves most of her budget to the ad. Your numbers will differ: the lesson is the method, not the figures.
Reach is not sales

Cheap reach only matters if the right people see you. 8,000 people who never throw parties are worth less than 300 who do. Always follow the funnel down to messages and orders before you decide a channel is working.
Digital marketing adds targeting, measurement and a low starting cost to traditional methods.
Owned, earned and paid media work best together; build owned channels first.

Your **target customer** is the specific kind of person most likely to buy from you and come back. Many small business owners say, 'My product is for everybody.' It may be true that anyone can use it, but you cannot afford to speak to everybody. Advertising platforms charge for every view, and a message written for everyone usually speaks to no one.

The last lens matters most for digital marketing. If your customers are traders in their 50s who live on WhatsApp and Facebook, a TikTok strategy will waste your energy. If they are university students, the opposite may be true. Do not guess: ask them.
Write a customer profile

A **customer profile** (marketers also call it a **persona**) is a short description of one typical buyer, written as if she were a real person. It keeps your posts consistent, because every time you write a caption you can ask, 'Would she care about this?' Base it on real conversations with your best customers, not on imagination.
Worked example: a customer profile for a meal-prep business
For example, Bisi cooks weekly meal packs in Abuja. She looks at her last 30 orders on WhatsApp and talks to six regular customers.
She notices 22 of the 30 orders came from women, most of them working in offices in Wuse and Garki.
In conversations, four of six say their biggest problem is coming home too tired to cook, and worrying that the family eats too much fast food.
Most order on Sunday evening after seeing her WhatsApp Status, and pay by bank transfer.

She writes the profile: 'Chioma, 34, works in an office in Wuse, two children, leaves home at 6:30am. Wants her family to eat home-style food on weekdays without cooking every night. Checks WhatsApp Status on Sunday evenings. Pays by transfer. Worries about hygiene and freshness.'
She writes her value proposition: 'Home-style Nigerian meals for busy Abuja families, cooked fresh on Sunday and delivered to your door.'
Bisi now posts her weekly menu on Sunday afternoon, shows her clean kitchen and packaging to answer the hygiene worry, and stops spending on adverts aimed at students who rarely order.
The value proposition

A **value proposition** is one sentence that says who you help, what you give them and why you are different. A useful pattern is: '[Product] for [target customer] who want [result], [what makes you different].' Avoid empty words such as 'quality' and 'best' unless you prove them. 'Delivered within 2 hours in Ikeja' is stronger than 'fast delivery'.
Talk to five customers

The fastest research is a short conversation, by phone or WhatsApp voice note, with five customers who have bought before. Keep it to about ten minutes. Ask open questions and listen more than you speak. Write their exact words down, because those words make the best captions later.
Five questions for a customer interview
How did you find us?
Why did you buy?
What nearly stopped you?
Where else did you look?
Who else should know?
These five questions reveal your best channel, your real selling point, your main objection and your referral path.
Respect privacy

Ask permission before you record a call or quote a customer by name in a post. Keep customer phone numbers and addresses private and use them only for the purpose you collected them for. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 requires businesses to handle personal data lawfully and securely.

You may find you have two or three groups, for example individual buyers and small shops that resell. That is fine. Write one profile for each, then choose one as your main focus for the next three months. You can expand later once the first group is working.
Common mistakes when defining customers
**Describing yourself instead of the buyer.** You may love bright colours, but your best buyers may prefer muted corporate styles. Let the orders decide.
**Choosing a group you cannot reach.** If you only deliver within Kaduna, a customer profile in Lagos is no use, however attractive.
**Never updating it.** Review your profile every few months. Customers change, and so do their favourite apps.
**Ignoring who pays.** For school uniforms, the child wears it but the parent pays. Speak to the person who makes the decision.
Marketing to everybody wastes money; pick a specific target customer.

Your **digital presence** is everything a customer finds when she looks for you online. Before you run adverts, make sure this presence is complete and trustworthy. Think of it as cleaning and stocking your shop before you invite people in. For most small businesses in Nigeria, the starter kit has four parts.

Social page attracts
Google profile gets found

Each channel sends customers towards the place where you take orders.
1. WhatsApp Business

**WhatsApp Business** is a free app from Meta, separate from ordinary WhatsApp, designed for small businesses. It lets you create a business profile with your address, hours, description, email and website, a **catalog** of products with photos and prices, automatic **greeting** and **away messages**, **quick replies** for common answers, and **labels** to sort customers. You can move your existing number to it, and your chats come with you. Lesson 3.4 covers it in depth.
2. Google Business Profile

A **Google Business Profile** is the free listing that appears on Google Search and Google Maps when someone searches for your business or for a service 'near me'. It shows your location or service area, phone number, hours, photos and reviews. Even home-based businesses can list a service area instead of a street address. Lesson 2.2 walks through it step by step.
3. One main social media page

Choose one platform where your target customer already spends time, usually Facebook, Instagram or TikTok, and do it well before adding a second. A business page on Facebook or a professional account on Instagram gives you free statistics (often called **insights**) and the ability to run ads later.
4. A link page or simple website

A website is not compulsory on day one, but you need one link that gathers everything. Options include a free link page, a simple site from a builder such as Google Sites or WordPress.com, or a store page from a payment provider. A website you control is owned media: no platform can suspend it. WhatsApp also gives every number a short link in the form wa.me/234XXXXXXXXXX (country code, then the number without the first zero), which opens a chat with you directly.
Consistency builds trust

Use exactly the same **business name, address and phone number** (marketers call this **NAP**) on every channel. If your Instagram says 'Tola's Kitchen', Google says 'Tolas Catering Services' and WhatsApp shows a different number, customers become unsure, and Google finds it harder to confirm your details. Use the same logo, colours and description everywhere too.
Worked example: setting up the kit for a tailoring business
For example, Funke runs a tailoring shop in Ogbomosho and currently uses only her personal WhatsApp.

Day 1: She installs WhatsApp Business on her phone and moves her number to it. She adds the shop name 'Funke Stitches', the category Clothing, her address, opening hours 9am to 6pm Monday to Saturday, and a description: 'Ankara, aso ebi and corporate wear made to measure in Ogbomosho. Ready in 7 days.'
Day 2: She photographs 12 finished outfits in daylight against a plain wall and adds them to her catalog with price ranges, for example 'Ankara gown from about ₦18,000'.
Day 3: She creates a Google Business Profile with the same name, address and phone number, adds the same photos and her hours, and requests verification.
Day 4: She converts her Instagram account to a professional account, uses the same name and logo, and puts her wa.me link in the bio.
Day 5: She asks five happy customers to leave an honest Google review.
In under a week Funke has a consistent presence: customers who find her on Instagram or Google can tap straight into a WhatsApp chat, see her catalog and know her hours before they ask.
Protect your accounts

Turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp settings and on your Facebook and Google accounts. Never share a verification code (OTP) with anyone, even someone claiming to be from Meta or Google. Anyone who gets your code can take over your account.

Finally, look at your presence as a stranger would. Search your business name on Google, open your profile on someone else's phone, and check every link. If anything is missing or out of date, fix it before you spend a single naira on promotion.
Good product photos on a phone

Shoot near a window in daylight, not under a yellow bulb. Use a plain background such as a white wall or a clean cloth. Wipe the camera lens first, hold the phone steady with both hands, and take the same angle for every product so your catalog looks tidy. Show size by placing the item next to something familiar, such as a hand.

Followers and likes feel good but do not pay rent. Marketers call numbers that look impressive but do not connect to sales **vanity metrics**. Keep them, but make your main goal about something closer to money: orders, bookings, enquiries or repeat customers.
Work backwards through the funnel

Once you have a sales goal, you can estimate how many people you need at each funnel stage. You need two numbers from your own history: what share of people who **message** you end up **buying**, and what share of people who **see** your content end up **messaging**. These shares are called **conversion rates**. If you have never measured them, track them for two weeks first, using tally marks in a notebook if needed.
From goal back to reach
40 orders (goal)
200 WhatsApp chats
10,000 people reached
Dividing the goal by each conversion rate tells you how wide the top of the funnel must be.
Worked example: how many people must Bisi reach?

For example, Bisi (the Abuja meal-prep seller) wants 40 orders in March. Her notebook from February shows: of every 100 people who chatted with her, 20 ordered. Her Status and Facebook insights suggest about 2 of every 100 people who see her posts send a message.
Chat-to-order conversion rate = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.
Chats needed = 40 orders ÷ 0.20 = 200 chats.
View-to-chat conversion rate = 2 ÷ 100 = 2%.
People to reach = 200 chats ÷ 0.02 = 10,000 people in March.
Her free posts reach about 4,000 people a month, so she needs about 6,000 more. She plans a small paid campaign and asks happy customers to share her menu.

Bisi now knows the size of the job. She also sees a cheaper route: if she raises her chat-to-order rate from 20% to 25% by replying faster and showing delivery times clearly, she needs only 160 chats and 8,000 people reached.
Improve the bottom first
It is usually cheaper to improve conversion (faster replies, clear prices, easy payment) than to buy more reach. Fix the leaks at the bottom of the funnel before pouring more people in at the top.
Your one-page 90-day plan
Goal: one SMART goal for the next 90 days.
Customer: one line from your customer profile.
Channels: two or three channels, each linked to a funnel stage.
Content and actions: what you will post or do each week, for example three posts and two Status updates weekly.
Budget: money for ads, data and printing, and hours per week. Spend only what you can afford to lose while you learn.
Measures: which numbers you will record each week and where (a notebook, Google Sheets or Excel).

Split 90 days into three months. Month one: build and test. Month two: keep what works and drop what does not. Month three: put more effort and money into the winners. Review your numbers every week, even for ten minutes, and write one sentence about what you learned.
Setting a sensible budget

There is no correct amount to spend on marketing. Start from what one customer is worth to you. If a meal pack earns Bisi about ₦3,000 profit after ingredients, packaging and delivery (an illustrative figure), she cannot spend more than ₦3,000 in advertising to win one order, or she loses money on it. In practice she should aim for much less, so the business still makes a profit. Lesson 4.3 calls this the **break-even cost per result**.

Count your free resources too. Time spent posting, replying and photographing is a real cost. If you can give marketing only five hours a week, plan for two channels done well, not five done badly. Write the hours into your plan next to the naira, and protect them in your week like a customer appointment.

Customers who search are already looking for what you sell, which makes search the warmest traffic you can get. This module explains how search engines decide what to show, how to appear on Google Maps, how paid search works, and how to measure what your marketing is really producing.

When a customer types 'aso ebi tailor in Ibadan' into Google, she gets a list of results in less than a second. Google does not search the whole internet at that moment. It searches its own giant library, called the **index**, which it has built in advance. Understanding how that library is built helps you get into it, and then rise towards the top. The general practice of earning better positions in free search results is called **search engine optimisation**, or **SEO**.
A person in front of a large search bar and result cards
Search engines match what people type with the pages in their index.
Three stages: crawl, index, serve
How Google Search works
Crawl: bots discover pages
Index: pages are stored and understood
Serve: best matches are ranked
Click: searcher visits you
Google describes these three stages in its own Search Central documentation.

**Crawling**: automated programs (Google's is called Googlebot) follow links from page to page and download what they find. A page that no other page links to, and that is not submitted to Google, may never be found.
**Indexing**: Google reads the text, images and structure of each page and stores what it is about. Pages that are blocked, very thin or duplicated may be left out.

**Serving and ranking**: when someone searches, Google picks the pages from its index it judges most relevant and useful, considering things like the words used, the searcher's location and language, the quality of the page and how well it works on a phone.

Small businesses usually win most easily on searches that include a **location** and a **specific product**, because big national brands do not compete hard for them. 'Cake' is impossible to win; 'birthday cake delivery Ikeja' is realistic.
Finding your keywords for free

**Keywords** are the words and phrases people type. Find them the way your customer would. Start typing your product into Google and note the suggestions that appear below the box (Google Autocomplete). Scroll down the results page for 'People also ask' and related searches. Ask customers what they would type. If you later open a Google Ads account, its free **Keyword Planner** tool shows rough search volumes.
Worked example: a keyword list for a cake business
For example, Ronke bakes cakes from home in Ikeja, Lagos, and wants her simple website and Google profile to be found.
She types 'birthday cake' into Google on her phone and notes suggestions such as 'birthday cake delivery' and 'birthday cake near me'.
She adds her area to each idea: 'birthday cake delivery Ikeja', 'custom cakes Ikeja', 'wedding cake Lagos'.
She asks five customers what they searched before finding her. Two say 'cake vendor in Ikeja', a phrase she had not thought of.
She chooses one main phrase per page: home page 'custom cakes in Ikeja', a second page 'wedding cakes in Lagos'.
She writes each page title, for example 'Custom Birthday Cakes in Ikeja | Ronke's Bakes', and uses the phrase naturally in the first paragraph and a photo caption.
Each page now has a clear topic matching real searches. Ronke avoids stuffing the same phrase into every sentence, which reads badly and does not help.
Basic on-page practice
Give every page a clear, unique **title** that includes the main phrase and your business name.
Write a short **description** (the summary under the title in results). Google may rewrite it, but a good one often gets used.
Use headings that say what each section is about, and write for people first.
Make sure the site works well on a phone and loads quickly on a slow connection: compress large photos before uploading.
Name photos sensibly (wedding-cake-ikeja.jpg, not IMG_2048.jpg) and add alt text describing them.
Register your site in **Google Search Console**, a free Google tool that shows which searches bring you visitors and flags problems.
Avoid shortcuts

Be wary of anyone who promises 'number one on Google in a week'. Buying links, copying other sites' text or hiding keywords can get pages pushed down or removed from results. Good SEO is slow and steady: useful pages, accurate details, real reviews.

If you have no website yet, the same ideas still apply to the places you do have. Your Google Business Profile description, your Facebook page 'About' section and your YouTube video titles are all read by search engines. Use the words your customers use, name your town, and describe exactly what you sell. 'Ankara gowns, aso ebi and school uniforms sewn in Ogbomosho' tells both people and search engines far more than 'Fashion is life'.
Google crawls, indexes and then ranks pages; a page must be found before it can rank.
Match your content to search intent: learn, find, compare or buy.
Local, specific phrases are the easiest for small businesses to win.

When someone searches 'pharmacy near me' or 'hair salon Surulere', Google often shows a map with three businesses under it before the normal results. Setting up your profile
Go to google.com/business on a browser, or open Google Maps and choose to add your business. Sign in with a Google account you will keep for the business.
Enter your business name exactly as customers see it on your signboard. Do not add extra keywords to the name; Google's guidelines forbid it.
Choose the most accurate **primary category**, for example 'Bakery' or 'Tailor'. You can add a few secondary categories.
Add your address if customers visit you. If you deliver or visit customers and work from home, hide the address and set a **service area** instead.
Add your phone number, your website or wa.me link, and your hours.

**Verify** the profile. Google offers different methods depending on the business, such as a phone or email code or a short video showing your location, signage and equipment. Your profile shows publicly only after verification.
Complete the profile fully

After verification, fill in everything: a description in plain language, products or services with prices where possible, opening hours including public holiday changes, and plenty of real photos. Add photos of the outside of the premises so people can recognise it, the inside, your team at work and your products. Use **posts** to share offers and news; they appear on your profile. Keep everything accurate: wrong hours are one of the quickest ways to lose a customer's trust.
How Google ranks local results
Google's three local ranking factors
Relevance: matches the search
Distance: close to the searcher
Prominence: well known and reviewed
Google's own help pages name these three factors for local results.

You cannot change **distance**, but you can improve the other two. **Relevance** improves when your category, description, products and services clearly match what people search. **Prominence** grows with reviews, ratings, photos and how well known your business is across the web, including links and mentions from other sites and directories.
Reviews: ask, respond, never fake

Reviews help both ranking and trust. In your profile you can copy a short link that takes customers straight to the review form. Send it to happy customers after delivery, with a simple message. Respond to every review, good or bad, politely and within a few days.
Worked example: asking for and answering reviews
For example, Halima runs a hair salon in Kano. She has 4 reviews and wants more.

After each appointment where the client seems happy, she sends on WhatsApp: 'Thank you for coming today! If you were happy with your hair, would you mind leaving us a short Google review? It helps other women find us: [review link].'
Over a month, about 1 in 4 clients she asks leaves a review. She asked 48 clients, so she gains about 12 reviews, taking her from 4 to 16.

One client leaves 2 stars, saying she waited 40 minutes. Halima replies: 'Thank you for telling us, Zainab. You are right that you waited too long, and we are sorry. We now confirm appointment times by WhatsApp the evening before. We would love to welcome you back.'
She checks her profile performance figures monthly: calls, direction requests and website clicks.
Halima's review count quadrupled with honest asking, and her calm reply to the negative review shows future clients that she listens. Many people read replies before choosing a business.
Fake and paid reviews break the rules

Do not write reviews for yourself, ask family to pretend to be customers, buy reviews, or offer discounts in exchange for reviews. Google's content policies prohibit fake engagement and incentivised reviews, and it can remove reviews or restrict profiles that break them. Also do not attack competitors with false reviews.
Using your profile performance data

Your profile shows how many people viewed it, and how many called, asked for directions or clicked to your website. Compare these with your sales. If views rise but calls stay flat, your photos, hours or description may not be convincing. If direction requests are high but few people arrive, check that your map pin is in the right place, and add a landmark to your description, such as 'opposite the First Bank on Allen Avenue'.

Finally, add your profile link to your WhatsApp Business profile, social bios and receipts, and check your profile at least once a month. Anyone can suggest edits to a public listing, so make sure your details have not been changed without your knowledge.
Google Business Profile is free and puts you on Google Search and Maps.
Use your real business name, the right category, accurate hours and real photos.
Local ranking depends on relevance, distance and prominence.
Ask happy customers for reviews and reply to all reviews; never fake or pay for them.

Paid search basics with Google Ads
Explain how pay-per-click search ads and the ad auction work
Choose keywords, match types and negative keywords
Write a search ad that matches the searcher's intent
Calculate clicks, cost per click and cost per order from a budget

SEO and Google Business Profile bring free visitors, but they take time. **Paid search** lets you appear at the top of results quickly by paying Google. The ads are marked 'Sponsored' and look similar to normal results. With Google Ads you usually pay only when someone **clicks**, which is why it is called **pay per click** (PPC).
A screen showing an online advert with a click cursor
Search ads appear when people type the words you choose.
How the ad auction works

Every time someone searches, Google runs a quick **auction** among advertisers who chose matching keywords. It does not simply give the top place to the highest bidder. Google considers your maximum bid, the quality and relevance of your ad and landing page, and the context of the search. Google Ads gives each keyword a **Quality Score** from 1 to 10, based on expected click-through rate, ad relevance and landing page experience. A relevant, useful ad can beat a bigger bid.
From search to sale with a search ad
Customer searches keyword
Auction picks ads
Your ad appears
Customer clicks (you pay)
Landing page converts
You pay at the click, so the page after the click must do its job.
Keywords and match types
Match type
How you write it
Broad match
cake delivery
Ads can show for searches related to the meaning, including wider ones. Reaches most people, least control.
Phrase match
"cake delivery"
Searches that include the meaning of the phrase, such as 'cake delivery in Ikeja'.
Exact match
[cake delivery ikeja]
Searches with the same meaning as the keyword. Most control, fewest searches.
Negative keyword
-recipe
Stops your ad showing when the search contains this word, so you do not pay for people looking for cake recipes.

For a small budget, start with a handful of phrase and exact match keywords that show buying intent, such as 'order', 'delivery', 'price' or a location. Add negative keywords for searches you do not want: 'free', 'recipe', 'jobs', 'training' or 'how to', unless those are your business.
Writing the ad

Google's standard text format is the **responsive search ad**: you supply up to 15 headlines (30 characters each) and up to 4 descriptions (90 characters each), and Google tests combinations. Include the keyword, a clear benefit, a reason to trust you and a call to action. Set **location targeting** to the area you actually serve, so you do not pay for clicks from people you cannot deliver to.
Headline ideas: 'Birthday Cakes in Ikeja', 'Same-Day Delivery Available', 'Order on WhatsApp Today'.
Description idea: 'Custom cakes baked fresh to order. Prices from about ₦25,000. Delivery across Ikeja and Maryland.'
Landing page: the page must show what the ad promised: photos, prices, delivery areas and a clear order button or WhatsApp link.
Worked example: what will a budget buy?

For example, Ronke sets a daily budget of about ₦5,000 for 20 days of a test campaign in Ikeja. Costs per click vary widely by industry and competition, so she uses her own results, not a guess. All figures are illustrative.
Total budget = ₦5,000 × 20 days = ₦100,000.
After the first week her report shows an average cost per click (CPC) of about ₦125. Clicks she can expect = ₦100,000 ÷ ₦125 = 800 clicks.
Her landing page converts 3% of visitors into orders (24 orders from her first 800 visitors in a similar earlier test). Expected orders = 800 × 0.03 = 24.
Cost per order = ₦100,000 ÷ 24 = about ₦4,167.
Her average profit per cake, before advertising, is about ₦9,000. Profit after ad cost per order = ₦9,000 − ₦4,167 = about ₦4,833.

The campaign is profitable, so Ronke keeps it running. If her conversion rate fell to 1%, she would get only 8 orders, costing ₦12,500 each, more than her profit per cake. That is why the landing page matters as much as the ad.

Start small and learn. Run a short test with a few tightly chosen keywords, check the **search terms report** in Google Ads after a few days to see the actual searches that triggered your ads, and add any wasteful ones as negative keywords. Pause keywords that spend money without producing enquiries. Only increase the budget when your cost per order is comfortably below your profit per sale.
How Google spends your daily budget

Google's help pages explain that on some days it may spend up to twice your average daily budget when there are more searches, but over a month it will not charge more than your daily budget multiplied by the average number of days in a month. Check your billing settings before you start and set an end date for tests.
Beware fake 'Google agents'

Google does not call or WhatsApp small businesses to demand payment for keeping their listing or ranking. Make payments only inside your own Google Ads account at ads.google.com, and never share your login or verification codes.
Search ads charge per click and appear for keywords you choose.
Ad position depends on bid and quality, not money alone.
Use specific, buying-intent keywords, location targeting and negative keywords.
Cost per order = total spend ÷ orders; it must be below your profit per sale.

UTM links: labelling your traffic

If you share your website link on Instagram, in a WhatsApp broadcast and in an email, how will you know which one brought the visitor? Add **UTM parameters**: small labels at the end of a link that analytics tools read. The three main ones are **utm_source** (where: instagram), **utm_medium** (what type: social, email) and **utm_campaign** (which promotion: easter_sale). Google offers a free Campaign URL Builder that assembles the link for you.
Worked example: tracking an Easter promotion
For example, Ngozi sells skincare from her website and promotes an Easter offer on three channels.
Instagram bio link: yoursite.com/easter?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=easter_sale
WhatsApp broadcast link: the same, but with utm_source=whatsapp&utm_medium=messaging
Email link: utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email
After two weeks, GA4 shows: Instagram 600 sessions and 12 purchases; WhatsApp 150 sessions and 9 purchases; email 200 sessions and 8 purchases.
Conversion rates: Instagram 12 ÷ 600 = 2%; WhatsApp 9 ÷ 150 = 6%; email 8 ÷ 200 = 4%.
Instagram brought the most visitors, but WhatsApp converted three times better. Ngozi decides to grow her WhatsApp broadcast list (with permission) and keep Instagram for awareness.
No website? Ask every customer

Many Nigerian small businesses sell entirely through WhatsApp, so analytics tools cannot see the sale. Ask every new customer, 'How did you hear about us?' and record the answer. In WhatsApp Business, use labels such as 'From Instagram' or 'From Google' to tag new chats. This simple habit is often the most valuable data you will have.
Your weekly tracking sheet

Create a sheet in Google Sheets or Excel, or a notebook page, with one row per week. Columns: people reached, profile or page visits, messages received, orders, revenue, money spent on ads, and the top source of new customers. Add two calculated columns: **chat-to-order rate** (orders ÷ messages × 100) and **cost per order** (ad spend ÷ orders from ads). Fill it every Monday for the previous week. After a month you will see trends that no single post can show.

Look for change over time, not single days. One quiet Tuesday means little; four weeks of falling messages means something. When a number moves, ask why, and write your guess in a notes column: a holiday, a price change, a new post style. Over time this notes column becomes your own marketing textbook.
A simple weekly review routine
Every Monday, open your sheet and your platform insights and fill in last week's row (about 15 minutes).
Compare with the week before and the same week last month. Mark any number that moved by a lot.
Find the channel that brought the most orders, not the most views, and note it.
Write one decision for this week, for example 'Post the menu on Status at 5pm instead of 9pm' or 'Pause the ad with the lowest click-through rate'.
Next Monday, check whether that decision changed the number you expected.
Numbers will never be perfect

Some customers see your Instagram post, search your name on Google a week later and then message you on WhatsApp. No tool records that whole journey. Accept that your data is approximate, and look for clear, repeated patterns rather than exact figures.
Keep your sheet private: it may contain customer names and phone numbers, which are personal data. Share only totals, not contact details, with anyone who helps you with marketing.

Content, social media, email and WhatsApp

Content is what you say; channels are where you say it. This module shows you how to plan useful content, choose and use social platforms with purpose, build an email list with permission, and turn WhatsApp from a chat app into an organised sales tool.
Content marketing: pillars, formats and a content calendar
Explain what content marketing is and how it moves people through the funnel
Choose three to four content pillars for your business
Turn one idea into several formats
Plan a two-week content calendar you can actually keep

**Content marketing** means attracting and keeping customers by sharing useful, interesting or entertaining material, rather than only shouting 'buy now'. A tailor who posts a short video on 'how to measure yourself for a gown' teaches something useful, shows her skill and reminds viewers she exists. When they need a gown, they think of her first.
A woman recording content on a phone with a ring light
Useful content builds trust long before a customer is ready to buy.
Content pillars

**Content pillars** are three or four themes you return to again and again. They stop you staring at your phone wondering what to post, and they make sure your content serves every stage of the funnel. Here is a set that works for most small businesses.
Pillar
Purpose
Funnel stage
Examples for a hair salon
Teach
Solve a small problem for free
How to protect braids at night; how long box braids should stay in
Show
Let people see how you work

Prove

Conversion
This week's price list; open slots for Saturday; a mid-week discount

Many marketers suggest that most posts should give value and only a minority should sell directly. Treat that as a rule of thumb, not a law. If every post is an advert, people stop watching. If none of them sell, people enjoy your posts but never know how to buy.
One idea, many formats

Creating content takes time, so get more from each idea. This is called **repurposing**. Formats include short vertical videos (Reels on Instagram and Facebook, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, WhatsApp Status), photos and carousels (several images in one post), text posts, voice notes, live videos, longer YouTube videos and blog articles. Short vertical video is currently a strong format on most social platforms, but photos and text still work, especially on WhatsApp and Facebook.
Worked example: repurposing one idea five ways
For example, Halima's salon gets the same question every week: 'How do I make my braids last longer?'
She records a 45-second vertical video at the salon, showing three tips: wrap with a satin scarf, moisturise the scalp lightly, avoid heavy oils.
She posts the video as an Instagram Reel and a TikTok, with the caption starting 'Want your braids to last 6 weeks? Do these 3 things.'
She shares the same video on WhatsApp Status that evening.
She turns the three tips into a 4-slide photo carousel for Facebook.
She saves the tips as a quick reply in WhatsApp Business, so when clients ask after appointments, she sends them in one tap.

One hour of work produced five pieces of content across four channels, all on her 'Teach' pillar. Her 'Sell' post that week links back: 'Book your braids before Saturday, and we will show you how to keep them neat.'
Your content calendar

A **content calendar** is a simple plan of what you will post, where and when. It can be a table in a notebook or Google Sheets. Batch your work: take photos and record videos on one day, write captions on another, and schedule posts in advance. **Meta Business Suite**, free from Meta, lets you schedule Facebook and Instagram posts ahead of time.
A realistic weekly content rhythm
Monday: Teach (short video)
Wednesday: Show (behind the scenes)
Friday: Prove (review or result)
Sunday: Sell (offer and prices)
Four planned posts a week, one per pillar, is sustainable for most busy owners.
Writing captions that work
Open with a hook in the first line, because that is often all people see before tapping 'more': a question, a number or a clear benefit.
Give the useful part quickly, in short sentences.
End with one clear **call to action**: 'Send us a WhatsApp message', 'Tap the link in our bio', 'Save this for later'.
Use a few relevant hashtags or location tags where the platform uses them, such as your city.
Use your customers' own words from your interviews in Lesson 1.2.
Permission and copyright

Ask clients before posting their faces or before-and-after photos, and respect a 'no'. Do not use other people's photos, videos or music as your own. Use your own photos, and for music use the licensed sound libraries inside the apps, which are made for that purpose.

Review your content once a month. In your insights, sort posts by saves, shares and the messages they produced, not only by likes. Look at the top three and ask what they have in common: a pillar, a format, a time of day, a type of hook. Make more of that, and quietly drop formats that took a lot of effort and brought nothing. Your calendar should change as you learn what your own customers respond to.
Content marketing attracts customers by being useful, not only by selling.

Reading the numbers
**Reach**: the number of different people who saw your content.
**Impressions** (Meta increasingly calls these **views**): the number of times it was shown, including repeats. Impressions are usually higher than reach.
**Engagement**: likes, comments, shares and saves. Saves and shares are especially valuable, because they show people found it useful enough to keep or pass on.
**Engagement rate**: engagements ÷ reach × 100. Platforms and tools define it slightly differently, so compare your own posts using the same formula each time.
Worked example: which post did better?
For example, Amaka compares two posts from her small chops page in Port Harcourt.
Post A, a photo of a platter: reach 2,000; 60 likes, 10 comments, 5 shares, 5 saves = 80 engagements.
Engagement rate A = 80 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 4%.
Post B, a short video packing an order: reach 1,200; 70 likes, 25 comments, 15 shares, 10 saves = 120 engagements.
Engagement rate B = 120 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 10%.
She also checks messages: Post A led to 3 WhatsApp enquiries, Post B to 9.
Post B reached fewer people but engaged far more, and brought three times the enquiries. Amaka plans more 'behind the scenes' packing videos and tracks whether the pattern holds over several weeks.
Community management

Social media is social. Reply to comments and direct messages quickly, ideally the same day. Answer price questions openly or move them politely to WhatsApp with a link; many customers are put off by 'Check DM' with no answer. Thank people who share your posts. Handle complaints calmly: acknowledge, apologise where appropriate, and offer to resolve in private. Delete spam and scam comments, especially fake accounts offering loans or 'customer support', which target your followers.
Watch for impersonators

Scammers sometimes copy a business's name and photos to create a fake page and collect payments. Tell customers clearly in your bio which account numbers and payment links are genuinely yours, ask followers to report fake pages, and report them to the platform yourself.
Profile checklist for any platform
A clear profile picture: your logo, or your face if you are the brand. It must be readable at small size.
A bio that says what you sell, where, and how to order, for example 'Small chops and finger foods for parties in Port Harcourt. Order on WhatsApp below.'
A contact button or link: your wa.me link, phone number or link page.
Pinned or highlighted posts showing prices, reviews and how delivery works, so new visitors do not have to scroll.
The same business name and handle on every platform where possible, so people can find you easily.

Finally, be consistent rather than constant. Three thoughtful posts a week, every week, build more trust than twenty posts in one excited week followed by a month of silence. Check your insights to find the days and times your followers are most active, and schedule posts for then.

Join the conversation beyond your own page too. Local Facebook groups for your area, estate or profession often allow business posts on certain days. Read the group rules first, contribute helpful answers, and only then share your offer. A helpful reply in a busy community group can bring more enquiries than a week of posts on a page with few followers.

Explain why an email list is valuable owned media
Collect email addresses with clear consent

Social platforms can change their rules, reduce your reach or suspend an account overnight. An **email list** is different: it is owned media, a list of people who have asked to hear from you. Email suits businesses with customers who use email regularly, such as professionals, organisations, training providers, online shops and anyone selling to other businesses.
An envelope with a campaign message flying out of a laptop
An email list is a channel you own and control.
Build the list with permission

Never buy email lists or add people without asking. It is disrespectful, damages your reputation with email providers so your messages land in spam, and conflicts with data protection principles. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, such as consent, for processing personal data. Ask clearly, say what you will send and how often, and make leaving easy.
A sign-up form on your website or link page, created with your email tool.
A tick-box on your order form: 'Send me monthly tips and offers by email' (not ticked in advance).
A **lead magnet**: something useful given in exchange for an email address, such as a price guide, a recipe booklet or a checklist.
At events and in your shop: a paper sign-up sheet that states what people are signing up for.
Choose a tool

Use an **email marketing service** rather than your personal Gmail. Examples include Mailchimp, Brevo and MailerLite; most offer free starter plans with limits on contacts or sends, so check the current terms on their sites. These tools provide sign-up forms, templates that display well on phones, an automatic **unsubscribe link** in every email, and reports. Many let you send a **welcome email** automatically when someone joins.

Give value first and regularly, and offers are welcomed rather than ignored.
Writing a good newsletter
**Subject line**: short and specific, telling the reader what is inside. 'Three ways to store your ankara so colours last' beats 'Newsletter No. 4'.
**Preview text**: the line shown after the subject in many inboxes; use it to add a reason to open.
**Body**: greet by first name if you have it, give one main useful item, keep paragraphs short, and add one or two good photos.
**One call to action**: a single clear button such as 'Shop the new collection' or 'Book a fitting'.
**Footer**: your business name, contact details and the unsubscribe link (your tool adds it).
Send a test to yourself and read it on your phone before sending to everyone.

Why open rates are less reliable now

Some email apps, notably Apple Mail with its Mail Privacy Protection feature, load email content automatically, which can count as an 'open' even if the person never read it. Clicks and sales are more trustworthy measures of success.

Your weekly posts and WhatsApp routine are **always-on marketing**: steady activity that keeps you visible. A **campaign** is different: a focused push with one objective, a clear offer, a start and end date and a budget. Good moments for campaigns include festive seasons such as Christmas, Eid and Easter, back-to-school, Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, the launch of a new product, or a quiet month you want to fill.
A team celebrating a product launch with a rocket

The one-page campaign brief

A **campaign brief** is a short document that answers every important question before you spend money. Even if you work alone, writing it forces clear thinking, and if someone helps you (a designer, a friend who runs your ads), it keeps everyone aligned.

Making an honest offer

An **offer** gives people a reason to act now rather than later. Good offers include a bonus (free embroidery, free delivery), a bundle (three uniforms for a set price), a deadline, or a limited quantity that is genuinely limited. Calculate the cost first: a 20% discount on a product with a 30% profit margin leaves you with very little. Bonuses that cost you little but are valued highly, such as free name embroidery, often work better than deep discounts.
Keep it truthful

Do not invent fake countdowns, fake 'only 2 left' messages or false 'was ₦20,000, now ₦10,000' prices. Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) protects consumers against misleading claims, and once customers catch one false claim, they stop trusting the rest.
The campaign timeline
Five phases of a four-week campaign
Week 0: brief and prepare
Week 1: tease and warm up
Weeks 2 to 3: launch and push
Final days: deadline reminder
After: review results
Preparation and review are part of the campaign, not extras.
**Prepare**: write the brief, take photos, design graphics, write captions and quick replies, check stock, set up UTM links and tracking.
**Tease**: hint at what is coming on Status and social media to build interest.
**Launch and push**: announce the offer on all channels, start ads, follow up enquiries daily.
**Deadline reminder**: one honest reminder 2 or 3 days before the offer ends often brings a burst of orders.
**Review**: compare results with the objective and write down what you learned for next time.
Worked example: splitting the budget and setting targets
For example, Maryam runs the uniform campaign in the brief above. She has about ₦50,000 to spend and a profit of about ₦3,500 per uniform order (illustrative figures).
Break-even cost per order = profit per order = ₦3,500. She wants to keep at least half, so her target cost per order is ₦1,750 or less.
Maximum orders she must win from paid channels to stay on target: ₦50,000 ÷ ₦1,750 = about 29 orders.
Her objective is 60 orders, so she expects about 31 to come from free channels: her broadcast list, Status and returning parents.
She splits money: ₦40,000 to a Facebook and Instagram ad over 3 weeks (about ₦1,900 a day) and ₦10,000 to flyers at two school gates with her WhatsApp QR code.
She adds a question to her order chat, 'Where did you see our offer?', and labels each chat by source.
Maryam knows before she starts what success looks like and the most she can pay per order. At the end she can say exactly which channel delivered.

Prepare your capacity too. A successful campaign can bring more orders than you can fulfil, and late deliveries create bad reviews. Check that you have materials, helpers and delivery arrangements for the number of orders in your objective, plus a little extra.

Finally, decide in advance what you will do if things go wrong. If by the end of week two you have far fewer enquiries than planned, will you change the offer, change the creative or move money to a better channel? Writing this 'if, then' plan in the brief stops you from panicking and spending more on something that is not working.

A **conversion** is whatever action counts as success for that campaign: an order, a booking, a form completed or a WhatsApp chat started. Be clear about which one you mean, because 'cost per result' in Ads Manager means cost per whatever result your campaign objective counts, which may be conversations rather than paid orders.
Worked example: a full campaign report
For example, Ngozi ran a Traffic campaign for her skincare website. Ads Manager and GA4 show the following. Figures are illustrative.
Spend ₦30,000. Impressions 60,000. Reach 20,000.
Frequency = 60,000 ÷ 20,000 = 3. Each person saw the ad 3 times on average.
Purchases (tracked with UTM links in GA4) 18. Conversion rate = 18 ÷ 900 × 100 = 2%. Cost per purchase = ₦30,000 ÷ 18 = about ₦1,667.

Each naira of advertising brought about ₦7.20 in sales. Whether that is profitable depends on her costs, which is the next step.
Revenue is not profit: break-even cost per result

ROAS uses revenue, but you also pay for products, packaging and delivery. Your **break-even cost per result** is the profit you make on one sale before advertising. If your cost per order is below it, the ad made money; above it, the ad lost money on that sale. In Ngozi's case, if each order costs her about ₦7,000 in products, packaging and delivery, her profit before ads is ₦12,000 − ₦7,000 = ₦5,000. Her cost per purchase of about ₦1,667 is well below ₦5,000, so each ad-driven order earned about ₦3,333 after ad costs, a total of about ₦60,000 profit from the campaign.
Break-even ROAS

You can also express break-even as a ROAS: average order value ÷ profit per order before ads. For Ngozi: ₦12,000 ÷ ₦5,000 = 2.4. Any ROAS above 2.4 makes money; below it loses money. Her 7.2 is comfortably above.

No marketer gets everything right the first time. The difference between businesses that grow and those that stall is a habit: try something, measure it, keep what works, change what does not, and repeat. This habit is called **iteration**. Done steadily, small improvements at each funnel stage multiply into large gains.

A/B testing

An **A/B test** compares two versions that differ in **one** thing only: the image, the headline, the offer, the audience or the posting time. If you change several things at once and results improve, you will not know which change helped. Meta Ads Manager has a built-in A/B test feature, but you can also test manually, as Amaka did with two ads in one ad set, or by alternating two WhatsApp follow-up messages.
**Test the big things first**: the offer and the main image or video usually matter more than button colour or small wording changes.

**Give it enough data**: a test with 5 clicks each tells you almost nothing. Wait until each version has had a fair number of results, and run tests for full weeks where possible, because weekdays and weekends behave differently.
**Write it down**: date, what you changed, the numbers and your decision. This log is your playbook.
Worked example: testing an offer
For example, Halima's salon tests two offers for quiet weekdays, each sent to half of her 200-person broadcast list over two weeks.
Version A, sent to 100 clients: '10% off all styles on Tuesday and Wednesday.' Bookings: 8.
Version B, sent to 100 clients: 'Free hot-oil treatment with any style on Tuesday and Wednesday.' Bookings: 14.
Booking rate A = 8 ÷ 100 = 8%. Booking rate B = 14 ÷ 100 = 14%.
Cost per booking: on an average style of about ₦15,000, 10% off costs her ₦1,500 per booking. The hot-oil treatment costs about ₦600 in products and 10 minutes of time.
She repeats the test with a new split the next fortnight; B wins again (13 bookings vs 7).
The free treatment brought more bookings and cost less per booking. Because the result held in a second round, Halima adopts it as her standard weekday offer.

**Scale gradually.** Large sudden jumps in budget can unsettle the ad system's learning and push costs up, so raise budgets in steps and check results after each step. Also check your capacity: doubling orders is only good if you can still deliver on time and maintain quality.
Growth beyond ads: lifetime value

Winning a customer once is expensive; keeping her is cheaper. **Customer lifetime value** (CLV) estimates how much profit one customer brings over the whole time she buys from you. A simple version: profit per order × orders per year × years she stays.
Example: Bisi's meal packs earn about ₦3,000 profit per order. A typical regular orders twice a month (24 times a year) and stays about 1.5 years.
CLV = ₦3,000 × 24 × 1.5 = ₦108,000 profit (illustrative).
So even paying ₦4,000 in ads to win a new regular customer is worthwhile, although it is more than the profit on her first order, as long as she becomes a regular.
Ways to raise CLV: excellent service, follow-up messages, a simple loyalty reward (for example, every 10th order includes a free dessert), and asking for referrals.
Referrals: your cheapest channel

Ask happy customers directly: 'If you know anyone who would enjoy this, please share my number.' A small thank-you for referrals, given to the customer who refers, is a common and honest practice. Track referrals with a label so you know how many new customers come this way.
